title: The boy who knew everything but this
hookLine: Shvetaketu comes home after twelve years of study, proud, and his father asks the one question he can't answer
carry: you are that: the self is never lost, only unseen

cards: In the Chandogya Upanishad, a boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Vedas. He comes back at twenty-four, having learned them all, and he walks in proud, sure he knows everything.
His father, Uddalaka, asks him one question. Did you ask for the teaching by which what hasn't been heard becomes heard, what hasn't been thought becomes thought, what isn't known becomes known?
Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. So his father gives a clue: know one lump of clay, and you know everything made of clay; the pots are only names. Shvetaketu admits it.
My teachers can't have known this, or they'd have told me. Please, sir, teach me. And lesson after lesson, his father ends on the same three words, usually rendered: you are that.

teach.b: Centuries later, Shankara opens his commentary on the Brahma Sutra with Shvetaketu's problem. The first line says: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. But is Brahman known already, or not?
If known, why inquire? If wholly unknown, how could anyone even want it? His answer: Brahman is known, in a way, because it is the self of everyone.
Nobody ever thinks, I am not. What's in doubt is what this self is. Some say the body, some the senses, some the mind, some a flicker of awareness, some a self that acts and enjoys.
Shvetaketu was just like that: full of learning, unclear about the one thing closest to him.
Shankara's own answer is the father's: the self, atman, is Brahman, the reality behind everything. That is the heart of Advaita Vedanta. So jnana isn't finding a new object.
It's clarity about what was never missing. Other Vedanta schools honor the same three words and read them differently; Ramanuja, for one, hears in them the Lord as the inner self of every self.
Today, plenty of people travel far to find themselves.

teach.h: THE ONE LOOKING IS THE ONE LOOKED FOR.
teach.b: This teaching turns the search around: the one looking is what's being looked for.

how: In Advaita Vedanta, students hear the Upanishads' great sayings, such as you are that, from a teacher, reflect on them, and sit with the question of what the self is; Shankara's commentary on the first sutra is a classic place to begin.

o: a list of rules for living as a student
the reward that comes from long rituals
knowing: becoming clear about the self

games.q: Shvetaketu and Shankara — tap the pairs.
p: twelve years of study, one thing missing
know it, and all clay is known

s: Shvetaketu came home humble, unsure of what he knew
he came home proud, sure he knew it all. his father's question showed what he'd missed.
for Shankara, nobody doubts that they exist
nobody ever thinks, I am not. the doubt is about what the self is.
every Vedanta school reads 'you are that' the same way
Shankara hears oneness with Brahman; Ramanuja hears the Lord as the inner self of every self.

games.q: your cousin says: i'm taking a gap year to go find myself. you've just heard Shvetaketu's story. what would Uddalaka point out?
o: good plan: the self is out there somewhere, waiting.
the one doing the looking is the self you're looking for.
the self is the body, so a trip won't change it.
games.why: travel all you like. on Shankara's reading, nobody ever lacks the self, only clarity about it. you are that.

practice: Sit comfortably and ask, quietly, the question many Advaita teachers give, made well-known by Ramana Maharshi: who am I?
Let the mind offer its answers, this body, these feelings, these thoughts, and let each one pass without deciding. Come back each time to the plain sense of being here, before any label.
If you pray, offer that plain presence; if you don't, simply rest in it.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing. On Shankara's reading of the first line, not finding something new, but becoming clear about a self that is never lacking.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the wish to know, from the same root as jnana; the key word of the Brahma Sutra's first line.

carryVoice: Your line: you are that: the self is never lost, only unseen. Shvetaketu knew everything but this. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–6.1.7 (Shvetaketu goes to study at twelve and returns at twenty-four, proud; the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard; the lump of clay; 'my teachers cannot have known this')
Chandogya Upanishad 6.8–6.16 (the refrain tat tvam asi, 'you are that')
Brahma Sutra 1.1.1 (now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman)
